entries.clue: Looking like a Teletubby with a sour expression? (2-5)

blocks.note: Po is one of the four Teletubbies, the small red one
-faced is the suffix that turns a word into a look: stony-faced, long-faced, so looking a certain way is being faced that way

annotation.surface: A children's television character caught in a thoroughly bad mood.
annotation.walkthrough: The enumeration does the telling: two letters then five, and the short chunk is a name. Po is the red Teletubby, while the sour sense comes from po the chamber pot, by way of poker-faced.
annotation.definitionFit: Po-faced means blank and humourless, wearing the disapproving look of someone determined not to be amused.

entries.clue: Without permission snaps A-lister’s breasts (4)

blocks.note: the tabloid verb: a photographer catches a celebrity unawares and sells the picture on
the old plural for a woman's breasts, the teat sense that survives now only in dialect

annotation.surface: Long-lens photographs of a famous person, taken with no consent asked for.
annotation.walkthrough: As a verb this is tabloid slang clipped from paparazzi, and it takes a celebrity as its object. The breast sense is medieval and survives in Scottish hill names like the Paps of Jura.
annotation.definitionFit: To pap someone is to photograph them uninvited, the paparazzo's trade; paps is separately an old plural for a woman's breasts, from the teat sense.

entries.clue: Tyson’s rage (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The first half is a possessive pointing at the surname of a British heavyweight boxer rather than offering a synonym.

blocks.note: the surname of the British heavyweight champion, the traveller's son from Manchester
the blazing sort of anger, hot and loud rather than cold

annotation.surface: The temper of a man called Tyson.
annotation.walkthrough: Tyson pulls you towards Mike, the American heavyweight; the setter means Tyson Fury, the British one, whose surname is the answer. A two-word clue is nearly always two definitions.
annotation.definitionFit: Fury is uncontrolled anger, plain rage, and it is also the surname carried by the boxer the clue names.

entries.clue: Meet to study a strip of grass (8)

blocks.note: to con something is to study it closely, the old sense kept alive in conning a lesson
the verge is the mown grass strip between a British road and its hedge

annotation.surface: Arranging to meet up and examine a lawn.
annotation.walkthrough: Con for study belongs to the same family as conning a ship's course. British roads are edged with verges, and councils argue every spring about when to cut them.
annotation.definitionFit: Lines that converge come together at a single point, which is what people do when they meet; both are plain present-tense verbs.

entries.clue: What’s definitely decided is cut with this (5)

annotation.definition: What’s definitely decided is cut with this

blocks.note: read as a matter already settled beyond argument, and meant as one half of the set phrase that says so
read as something being sliced by a tool, and meant as naming the word that sits beside 'cut' in that phrase

annotation.surface: Something already settled being sliced open with an unnamed implement.
annotation.walkthrough: Cut and dried comes from the herbalist's trade: herbs cut and then dried were ready prepared for sale over the counter, as against gathered fresh. The clue hands you 'cut' and asks for its partner.
annotation.definitionFit: The answer is the second half of 'cut and dried', the phrase for a matter settled in advance, and the clue supplies the first half.

entries.clue: Material is wonderful and no end costly (6)

indicatorNotes.no end: Something arriving with no end has lost its last part, so the final letter of the word beside it is left off.

blocks.note: fab is the sixties clipping of fabulous, meaning wonderful
costly is RICH, and the H at its end comes off

annotation.surface: Something both wonderful and endlessly expensive.
annotation.walkthrough: No end reads as 'endlessly' in the surface and as an instruction in the wordplay. Fab has meant wonderful since the Beatles were the Fab Four.
annotation.definitionFit: Fabric is woven cloth, the stuff a garment or a curtain is made from, which is material in the everyday tailoring sense.

entries.clue: The river that moves vast quantities of goods (6)

annotation.definition2: that moves vast quantities of goods

blocks.note: the South American giant, carrying more water to the sea than any other

blocks.clueFragment: that moves vast quantities of goods
blocks.note: the retailer named after it, shifting parcels out of warehouses the size of villages

annotation.surface: A great waterway carrying cargo across a continent.
annotation.walkthrough: One name serves twice, because the retailer was christened after the river for exactly the reason the clue gives: both shift more than anything else of their kind.
annotation.definitionFit: The Amazon is the vast river draining South America; Amazon is also the online retailer whose warehouses move goods by the containerload.

entries.clue: Later I failed to leave car in out-of-town centre (6,4)

indicatorNotes.failed: Something that has failed has not come out as it should, so the letters beside it have not come out in their given order either.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder, re-set
to park is to leave a car standing somewhere

annotation.surface: A driver admitting that they later failed to park at the shopping centre.
annotation.walkthrough: The signal sits between the fodder and the second chunk, where an innocent 'failed to leave' would go. A retail park is the British cluster of big sheds beside a ring road, ringed by free parking.
annotation.definitionFit: A retail park is a shopping development built beyond the edge of a town, where land is cheap and everybody arrives by car.

entries.clue: Remember: ring for the babysitter? (4,2,4)

blocks.note: to ring somebody is to call them
what the babysitter is there for is to mind the children

annotation.surface: A note to yourself about telephoning the sitter.
annotation.walkthrough: The colon makes the clue read as a to-do list, which hides the join: the second half says what a babysitter is for, not who they are. Mind for look after is everyday British — mind the baby, mind my bag.
annotation.definitionFit: To call something to mind is to summon it back into your thoughts, which is what remembering is; both are verbs in the infinitive.

entries.clue: Airborne soldier without his dog tag is unnecessarily fearful (8)

blocks.note: a para is a paratrooper, the soldier who arrives by parachute
to be without a thing is to have no thing
a dog tag is the stamped metal disc carrying a soldier's identification

annotation.surface: A paratrooper who has lost his identity disc.
annotation.walkthrough: Without does the work of a whole chunk here rather than merely joining two. Dog tags are worn in pairs on a chain, one to stay with the body and one to be collected.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone paranoid is gripped by suspicions and fears that nothing justifies, which is being fearful unnecessarily.

entries.clue: Meat spread left in light shade (6)

blocks.note: meat paste is the potted spread sold in small jars for sandwiches
L is the standard abbreviation for left

annotation.surface: Sandwich spread left out in a dim corner of the kitchen.
annotation.walkthrough: Left is the abbreviation rather than the past tense of leave, and that swap is the one thing the clue asks you to spot. Meat paste is a British teatime relic, sold beside the fish paste.
annotation.definitionFit: Pastel names the pale, milky end of any colour — powder blue, primrose — so a pastel is a light shade of it.

entries.clue: The pack, or a whole team (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The first half is a collective noun standing in for its members: the singular group names the plural animals that make it up.

blocks.note: the hunting group, read as the collective and meant as the animals inside it
the nickname of Wolverhampton Wanderers, used of the side and of the club alike

annotation.surface: Animals hunting together, or the eleven who run out on a Saturday.
annotation.walkthrough: A whole team hints that the second reading is a name and not a description. Wolves is Wolverhampton Wanderers, the Midlands football club, and supporters use the nickname for the side as well as the club.
annotation.definitionFit: A pack is the hunting group wolves live in, so the collective names the animals; Wolves is also the nickname of an English football club.

entries.clue: Send girl to do work for tree specialist (12)

indicatorNotes.work: To work a material is to knead and press it into some other shape, and letters worked like that come out in a new order.

blocks.note: twelve letters of fodder

annotation.surface: Telling a young woman to go off and do a job for somebody.
annotation.walkthrough: The signal hides inside 'to do work for', which is how you would phrase an errand. Dendron is Greek for tree, the root behind rhododendron and dendrite.
annotation.definitionFit: A dendrologist is the botanist whose field is trees — their species, growth and identification — which is what a tree specialist studies.

entries.clue: Warmly received, returning to pavilion, exhausted (7,3)

blocks.note: a performance warmly received is clapped
in cricket a batter who is out walks back to the pavilion

annotation.surface: A cricketer applauded all the way back to the pavilion.
annotation.walkthrough: The pavilion is the clubhouse beside a cricket field, and a dismissed batter is out — the word wanted, though the surface is only about the walk. Clapped out is usually said of an old car.
annotation.definitionFit: Something clapped out is worn past the point of working, and said of a person it means exhausted, with nothing left to give.

entries.clue: Vaguely outlined throwing mud at beard (10)

indicatorNotes.throwing: Throwing a handful of something scatters it, and letters that have been scattered land in a different order.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder

annotation.surface: Slinging handfuls of mud at a bearded man.
annotation.walkthrough: Throwing mud is a phrase in its own right, smearing somebody's name, which is why the instruction hides so well. Adumbrate is from the Latin umbra, shadow: to sketch a thing as its shadow.
annotation.definitionFit: To adumbrate something is to sketch it in faint outline and no more, so adumbrated is the state of having been vaguely outlined.

entries.clue: She dropped everything to tour Midlands town (4,6)

annotation.definition: She dropped everything to tour Midlands town

blocks.note: read as abandoning whatever she was busy with, and meant as taking off every stitch she was wearing
read as a sightseeing trip round the region, and meant as the ride through Coventry the legend puts her on

annotation.surface: A woman abandoning her plans to go sightseeing in the Midlands.
annotation.walkthrough: Dropped everything means her clothes, not her plans. The legend has her ride naked through Coventry to shame her husband into cutting the town's taxes, and Peeping Tom is the man who looked.
annotation.definitionFit: Lady Godiva is the Coventry noblewoman of legend who rode the length of the town wearing nothing at all, which is what every word here describes.

entries.clue: Put out needing two days to cross river (6)

indicatorNotes.cross: To cross a river is to pass over it from one bank to the other, so whatever crosses it finishes up on both sides of it.

blocks.note: a day is D, and the clue asks for two of them: here is the first
the Ouse is an English river, one that runs through York
the second of the two days, closing the word off

annotation.surface: A job that will take a couple of days and a river crossing.
annotation.walkthrough: The Ouse is the crossword setter's favourite river, four letters with three of them vowels. Douse is what you do to a flame with a bucket of water.
annotation.definitionFit: To douse a fire is to put it out with a bucket of water or a sharp smothering, and both words here are past forms.

entries.clue: Cannon and Ball (3-3)

blocks.note: the quick-firing naval gun of both world wars, named for the noise it made
the woollen bobble sewn on a hat, or the shaker a cheerleader waves

annotation.surface: The billing of an old-fashioned variety double act.
annotation.walkthrough: Cannon and Ball were a British comedy double act, and that is the whole of the surface. The gun took its name from the noise it made firing, and the woolly ball is the one sewn on a bobble hat.
annotation.definitionFit: A pom-pom was the two-pounder automatic gun of the world wars, a cannon; a pom-pom is equally the ball of wool on a hat or a cheerleader's shaker.

entries.clue: Clubs embracing in-your-face charity collection (8)

blocks.note: C is clubs, the card suit's abbreviation on a bridge scoresheet
to embrace someone is to hug them

annotation.surface: Nightclubs throwing their arms around a pushy fundraising drive.
annotation.walkthrough: Clubs is the card suit here, not a nightclub or a weapon. Chugging is short for charity mugging, the British name for the clipboard fundraisers who step into your path on the high street.
annotation.definitionFit: Chugging is signing passers-by up to direct debits by blocking their way, so the definition catches both the pushiness and the good cause behind it.

entries.clue: See 17
Like the part of Africa that is below the sand? (3-7)

blocks.note: the prefix sub- means below or beneath, as in submarine and subsoil
the sand is the Sahara, the desert spanning north Africa, and Saharan is its adjective

annotation.surface: A guess at which stretch of Africa lies underneath the desert sand.
annotation.walkthrough: Below is a map word: with north at the top of the page, below the desert means south of it rather than underneath it. The Sahara runs from the Atlantic to the Red Sea, and the countries south of it are the ones meant.
annotation.definitionFit: Sub-Saharan describes the African countries lying south of the great desert, the sense of 'below' you read off a map rather than a depth.

entries.clue: Material for path of serious length (6)

blocks.note: a grave matter is a serious one
L is the standard abbreviation for length

annotation.surface: Choosing what to lay on a very long garden path.
annotation.walkthrough: Of serious length reads as one phrase in the surface and splits into two pieces in the wordplay. L for length is the letter on a clothing label or a plan's specification.
annotation.definitionFit: Gravel is the loose stone chippings rolled flat to surface a drive or a garden walk, so it is what such a path is made of.

entries.clue: Faulty information on the computer (5,7)

blocks.note: what is faulty about a piece of work is its error
a message is a piece of information passed along

annotation.surface: A computer announcing that something has gone wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word does double duty: the sentence describes the thing and spells it at the same time, so no word is left over to act as a separate definition. Only 'on the computer' sits outside the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue is what pops up when a machine hits a fault: information telling you what has gone wrong.

entries.clue: Strength of wines intoxicated (5)

indicatorNotes.intoxicated: Somebody intoxicated cannot walk a straight line, and letters in that condition do not keep to the order they were given.

blocks.note: five letters of fodder

annotation.surface: A cellar's worth of wine gone to somebody's head.
annotation.walkthrough: Strength of wines reads as one phrase, how strong the bottles are, which is what keeps the fodder out of sight. Sinew is tendon, the tough white cord tying muscle to bone.
annotation.definitionFit: Sinew is tough tendon, and by extension the word means muscular power, strength in the sense of what holds a body together.

entries.clue: Scrap part of an alphabet (4)

blocks.note: the smallest bit of a thing, as in not one scrap of evidence
a single Greek letter, ninth of the twenty-four and the shortest to write

annotation.surface: A fragment salvaged from some ancient writing system.
annotation.walkthrough: Iota is the ninth Greek letter, a single vertical stroke and the smallest of them, which is how it came to mean the smallest possible amount. Not one iota keeps that sense in use.
annotation.definitionFit: An iota is the tiniest Greek letter, so it stands for the least scrap of anything; it is also a letter of that alphabet in its own right.

entries.clue: Phone to America from prison (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The second half names the building for the room inside it: what a prisoner is locked in, rather than the whole establishment.

blocks.note: the American word for a mobile, clipped from cellular
the locked room an inmate lives in, a sense borrowed from the monastery

annotation.surface: An inmate ringing the States from inside.
annotation.walkthrough: To America is not the direction of the call: it tells you whose word is wanted, the American clipping of cellular. Prisoners are not allowed mobiles, which is what makes the surface a joke.
annotation.definitionFit: In America a mobile phone is a cell, short for cellular; a cell is equally the small locked room a prisoner lives in.

entries.clue: An interval before VAT comes back reduced (6)

indicatorNotes.reduced: A phrase reduced is cut down to a piece of itself, so only a short run of the letters written out here is taken.
indicatorNotes.back: Something that comes back is travelling the other way, so the run of letters is read from its end to its start.

blocks.note: the run E-V-A-T-C-O lies across the ends and starts of these three words, and is taken in the other direction

annotation.surface: Waiting for the tax bill to come back smaller than last time.
annotation.walkthrough: The hidden run straddles three words and needs both instructions at once, which is why 'comes' belongs to the letters and 'back' to the signal. VAT is Britain's value added tax, the one on every till receipt.
annotation.definitionFit: An octave is the gap between a note and the next one bearing the same name, eight steps up the scale, which makes it a musical interval.

entries.clue: Religious leader who’s gone off the record (8)

annotation.definition: Religious leader who’s gone off the record

blocks.note: to have gone off something is to have turned against it, to be anti it
the pope leads the Roman Catholic church

annotation.surface: A churchman briefing reporters on condition that nobody quotes him.
annotation.walkthrough: Off the record is the journalist's phrase on the surface and the literal truth underneath: these claimants are the ones left out of the Vatican's official list. The last of them gave up his claim in 1449.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes a rival claimant to the papacy who never made it onto the official roll of popes.

entries.clue: Very small, or a little high (6)

blocks.note: the nursery word for tiny, the one behind tiddler
gently drunk, the state a sherry or two leaves you in

annotation.surface: Something no size at all, or somebody pleasantly merry.
annotation.walkthrough: A little high is the drink sense, nothing to do with height or narcotics. Tiddly for tipsy comes from tiddlywink, old slang for an unlicensed beershop; the small sense is the nursery one behind tiddler.
annotation.definitionFit: Tiddly is nursery talk for tiny, and in British use it equally means gently drunk — a couple of sherries rather than a session.

entries.clue: What dogs do, pleased to see bird (7)

blocks.note: what a happy dog does is wag
a dog pleased to see you wags one thing, and that is its tail

annotation.surface: A dog greeting its owner at the front door.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma keeps the clue reading as one sentence about dogs, which hides the join before the definition. A wagtail is the small black-and-white bird that pumps its long tail up and down as it walks beside British rivers.
annotation.definitionFit: The wagtail is a slender bird named for the constant flicking of its long tail, so the one-word definition is the plain dictionary one.
